cues.text:
Pastry chef Nicolas Appert was looking
for a way to preserve food for longer.

In Brest, food prepared by his method
remained in sealed vessels

for three months at the roadstead, an anchorage
near the port.

When the Board of Health
inspected the food,

the broth, meat, beans, and green peas received
a favorable assessment.

For the early nineteenth century,
this was an unusual result.
But preserving a few samples

and teaching other people to get the same
result were different challenges.
How could one person turn years of experiments
into a method others could use?

At the time, people preserved food
mainly with salt, sugar, and drying.

These methods extended shelf life, but changed
the food’s taste and qualities.

Appert, who worked as a pastry chef
and distilled spirits, looked for another way.

He experimented with meat, broth, milk,
vegetables, and fruit.
He left prepared samples in storage,

then checked their condition later
to find out which methods had worked.

His method relied on glass bottles
and wide-mouthed vessels.

Appert filled them with food,
sealed them with corks,

fastened the corks with wire,
and heated the vessels in a water bath.

Different foods required different preparation
and heating times.

The shape of the neck, the quality of the glass,
and the seal all mattered.
A bottle could burst while heating.

Appert put the vessels in cloth bags
to contain the shards.
Green peas created another problem:

peas picked too young became too soft after
processing.
In March 1809, a committee

of the Society for the Encouragement
of National Industry inspected

samples prepared by Appert and gave their
condition a favorable assessment.

Appert reported that some foods
had been prepared

more than eight months earlier, and one sample
fifteen months before the inspection.

But the society had kept the vessels for only
about two months.

The committee could assess the food’s
condition,

but had not observed the entire storage period
Appert described.

The proposal to publish a detailed account
of the method came from Appert himself.

On January 30, 1810, France’s minister
of the interior sent him a letter.
It set out a reward of twelve thousand francs

on the condition
that Appert prepare and publish

a description of his method
and provide the ministry with two hundred copies.

The description was to be submitted
to the Board of Arts and Manufactures

for consideration,
and Appert had to pay for printing himself.

Appert described
how to work with different foods:

their preparation, the tools required,
and the steps to follow.
He explained the vessels, corks,

heating times, and mistakes that could affect
the result.

In 1810, Appert’s book appeared
in France,

turning years of individual work
into a published guide.
